parole.significato: A suffix found in place names of Slavic origin, especially in northeastern Germany

parole.testo: Derived from Proto-Slavic *-oviťь, rebracketing it as -o- + -witz. Compare Polish -owicz.

parole.significato: dormouse (umbrella term for rodents of the family Gliridae)
parole.testo: From Middle High German bilch, pilch, from Old High German bilch, pilch, bilich, pilich, an early borrowing from Proto-Slavic *pъlxъ.

parole.significato: a type of sweet pastry similar to pancakes

parole.testo: Not attested in the core period of Middle High German. Found in Old High German as tirnboum, tyrn, presumably a borrowing from Proto-Slavic *dernъ (“cornel, dogwood”).

From Middle High German krechse. Further origin uncertain. One theory derives it from Proto-Slavic *krošňa (“basket”). If so, it would have to be an early borrowing predating both secondary umlaut and the Middle High German development of /sx/ > /ʃ/. Whatever its origins, the word most likely intera

parole.significato: horseradish (plant of the mustard family, Armoracia rusticana)
parole.testo: From Middle High German krēn, krēne, chrēn. Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *xrěnъ via a Slavic language like Czech křen (compare Silesian East Central German Krên), used in southern Germany and Austria.

parole.significato: innkeeper, tavernkeeper, pubkeeper (male or of unspecified gender)
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *kъrčьmařь from *kъrčьma + *-ařь, or an analogous form in an early western daughter language of Proto-Slavic.

Inherited from Middle High German kürsenære, from Old High German kursināri, derived from kursina, a borrowing from Proto-Slavic *kъrzьno. Equivalent to obsolete Kürsen, Kürschen (“fur coat / furcoat”) + -er.

From Middle High German *Pole or *Polen (attested as Polen m pl), from Old Polish polanín, from Proto-Slavic *poľaninъ (literally “field-dweller”), derived from *pȍľe (“field”). The Middle High German form may have been a strong noun in -en in light of polnisch; the weak form is then a backformation
From Middle High German, via Old Sorbian *ukleja from Proto-Slavic *uklěja.

parole.significato: siskin, especially the Eurasian siskin (Spinus spinus)
parole.testo: From Middle High German zīsec, zīsic. Cognate with Czech čížek (“siskin”). Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *čižь.

From Middle High German zisel, probably ultimately from Proto-Slavic *sysьlъ. Forms ending in Maus (“mouse”) were formerly more common: Old High German zisimūs, Middle High German zisemūs, and German Zieselmaus.
From Middle High German zülle, probably ultimately from Proto-Slavic *čьlnъ. Doublet of Schinakel. Compare Bavarian Zün.

19th century, from East Central German dialects. Further origin uncertain. Plausibly from Polish kleć (“outhouse”), from Proto-Slavic *klětь. Alternatively from klitschen (“to splat, slap”), a variant of klatschen.
